stemMd: A cough syrup has a density of $1.3\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$. What is its density in $\text{kg/m}^{3}$?
explanationMd:
**Method.** Convert the numerator and the denominator separately. $1\ \text{g}=10^{-3}\ \text{kg}$, and since $1\ \text{cm}=10^{-2}\ \text{m}$, $1\ \text{cm}^{3}=(10^{-2})^{3}\ \text{m}^{3}=10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}$. So

$$1.3\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^{3}}=1.3\cdot\frac{10^{-3}\ \text{kg}}{10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}}=1.3\times 10^{3}\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^{3}}.$$

**How to check it.** Water, $1\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$, is $1000\ \text{kg/m}^{3}$ (a cubic metre of water has a mass of one tonne). A syrup $1.3$ times as dense is $1300\ \text{kg/m}^{3}$.

distractorRationale.b: Converts only the volume, $\text{cm}^{3}\to\text{m}^{3}$, and leaves the mass in grams: $1.3\times 10^{6}$ is the density in $\text{g/m}^{3}$.
distractorRationale.d: Converts only the mass, $\text{g}\to\text{kg}$, and leaves the volume in cubic centimetres: this is the density in $\text{kg/cm}^{3}$.
distractorRationale.a: Uses $1\ \text{m}^{3}=100\ \text{cm}^{3}$, applying the length factor $10^{2}$ instead of cubing it.
distractorRationale.e: Confuses the cubic metre with the litre: $1.3\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$ is $1.3\ \text{kg/L}$, but a cubic metre holds $1000$ litres.

accessibilityText: A cough syrup has a density of 1.3 grams per cubic centimetre. Express it in kilograms per cubic metre. The five choices are: 0.13; 1.3 times 10 to the 6th; 1.3 times 10 to the 3rd; 1.3 times 10 to the minus 3; 1.3; all in kilograms per cubic metre.

provenance.notes: Original item on converting a density between units, with the volume factor cubed. Distractors convert only one of the two units, forget to cube, or confuse the litre with the cubic metre.

review.author: tolc-f-wave8-mpl-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: 1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3, so 1.3 g/cm^3 = 1.3x10^3 kg/m^3. 10^6 and 10^-3 come from wrong exponents; 1.3 and 0.13 ignore the conversion. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-tolcf-mpl-run1) reached the same answer: 1 g/cm^3 = 10^-3 kg / 10^-6 m^3 = 10^3 kg/m^3, so 1.3x10^3 kg/m^3. 10^6 and 10^-3 come from using only one of the two factors or inverting them.]

it.stemMd: Uno sciroppo per la tosse ha una densità di $1.3\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$. Qual è la sua densità in $\text{kg/m}^{3}$?
it.explanationMd:
**Metodo.** Converti separatamente il numeratore e il denominatore. $1\ \text{g}=10^{-3}\ \text{kg}$, e poiché $1\ \text{cm}=10^{-2}\ \text{m}$, $1\ \text{cm}^{3}=(10^{-2})^{3}\ \text{m}^{3}=10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}$. Quindi

$$1.3\ \frac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^{3}}=1.3\cdot\frac{10^{-3}\ \text{kg}}{10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{3}}=1.3\times 10^{3}\ \frac{\text{kg}}{\text{m}^{3}}.$$

**Come verificarlo.** L'acqua, $1\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$, ha densità $1000\ \text{kg/m}^{3}$ (un metro cubo d'acqua ha una massa di una tonnellata). Uno sciroppo $1.3$ volte più denso ha densità $1300\ \text{kg/m}^{3}$.

distractorRationale.b: Converte solo il volume, $\text{cm}^{3}\to\text{m}^{3}$, e lascia la massa in grammi: $1.3\times 10^{6}$ è la densità in $\text{g/m}^{3}$.
distractorRationale.d: Converte solo la massa, $\text{g}\to\text{kg}$, e lascia il volume in centimetri cubi: questa è la densità in $\text{kg/cm}^{3}$.
distractorRationale.a: Usa $1\ \text{m}^{3}=100\ \text{cm}^{3}$, applicando il fattore delle lunghezze $10^{2}$ invece di elevarlo al cubo.
distractorRationale.e: Confonde il metro cubo con il litro: $1.3\ \text{g/cm}^{3}$ equivale a $1.3\ \text{kg/L}$, ma un metro cubo contiene $1000$ litri.

it.accessibilityText: Uno sciroppo per la tosse ha una densità di 1,3 grammi per centimetro cubo. Esprimila in chilogrammi per metro cubo. Le cinque alternative sono: 0,13; 1,3 per 10 alla sesta; 1,3 per 10 alla terza; 1,3 per 10 alla meno 3; 1,3; tutte in chilogrammi per metro cubo.
